label: Place
name: Jakarta
summary:
Jakarta, officially the Special Region of Jakarta, is the de facto capital and largest city of Indonesia, located on the northwest coast of Java. With 10.5 million people in the city and 33 million in the metropolitan area (Greater Jakarta), it is the second-largest urban agglomeration in the world. Jakarta is being replaced as Indonesia's capital by the new city of Nusantara in Borneo, a relocation driven by Jakarta's catastrophic land subsidence — the city is sinking at up to 25 cm per year in some districts, partly submerged by 2050 under current projections.

The site was an important Sunda Kingdom trading port called Sunda Kelapa for centuries before the Portuguese arrived in 1513. In 1527, the Demak Sultanate's admiral Fatahillah captured and renamed it Jayakarta. The Dutch East India Company (VOC) seized Jayakarta in 1619, renamed it Batavia, and made it the administrative capital of the Dutch East Indies — the most profitable colonial trading empire of the 17th century. Batavia's harbor was the hub of the spice trade connecting Europe, India, China, and the Indonesian archipelago.

Japanese occupation (1942–1945) and Indonesian independence (1945) transformed Batavia into Jakarta. Under Sukarno and then Suharto's New Order (1967–1998), Jakarta grew explosively as millions migrated from Java's rural areas. The 1998 Indonesian Reformasi uprising that ended Suharto's dictatorship was centered in Jakarta's streets — one of Asia's most consequential democratic transitions of the 20th century.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: As a major trading port and later capital of Indonesia, Jakarta played a significant role in shaping regional trade networks and Dutch colonial expansion. The city's catastrophic land subsidence poses a pressing environmental challenge for the region.

Indonesian independence (1945) transforming Batavia into Jakarta as the capital of the world's fourth-most populous nation
Suharto's New Order (1967–1998) fueling Jakarta's explosive growth through centralized development spending
Land subsidence crisis (ongoing) — Jakarta sinking due to groundwater extraction, driving the decision to build a new capital
effects: Second-largest urban agglomeration in the world (33 million in Greater Jakarta)
1998 Reformasi uprising centered in Jakarta ending Suharto's 32-year dictatorship and beginning Indonesia's democratic transition
Capital relocation to Nusantara in Borneo — one of the world's most ambitious and controversial capital-city moves
Dutch colonial Batavia as the center of VOC's commercial empire — shaping Indonesian, Javanese, and global spice trade history
